Purified
PYOOR-i-fide
v. (past part.)
From Latin purificare, to make pure, from purus (clean, unmixed) and facere (to make). Webster 1828: freed from foreign or heterogeneous matter; cleansed from guilt or the defilement of sin. The metallurgical image — ore purified in the furnace — stands behind most of the biblical usage.

Biblical Definition

Purified in Scripture describes what God does to the inside of a man, and the New Testament is emphatic that the instrument is faith and the agent the Spirit, never ceremony. Peter reports the Jerusalem council’s decisive argument about the Gentiles: God gave them the Holy Ghost, And put no difference between us and them, purifying their hearts by faith (Acts 15:9). The heart is the object, faith the means, and the same work in Jew and Gentile alike — which ended the question of circumcising the nations. Peter says the same to the scattered churches: Seeing ye have purified your souls in obeying the truth through the Spirit unto unfeigned love of the brethren, see that ye love one another with a pure heart fervently (1 Peter 1:22). Purity is not privacy; its stated end is love of the brethren, and a man who claims a purified soul and hates his brother has disproved his claim. The purchase price was the death of Christ: Who gave himself for us, that he might redeem us from all iniquity, and purify unto himself a peculiar people, zealous of good works (Titus 2:14). And the hope of seeing Him works backward into present conduct: every man that hath this hope in him purifieth himself, even as he is pure (1 John 3:3). Daniel adds the furnace: Many shall be purified, and made white, and tried (Daniel 12:10).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines PURIFIED as freed from extraneous matter; cleansed; freed from guilt or the defilement of sin; and, in the ceremonial sense, freed from legal uncleanness by the appointed rites.

expand to see more

PURIFIED, pp. — Freed from foreign or heterogeneous matter; cleansed; refined, as metal in the furnace.

Freed from guilt or the defilement of sin; made holy in heart and life.

In the ceremonial sense, cleansed from legal pollution by the rites appointed under the law.

Cleared from improper mixture or corruption; as, a purified language or a purified worship.

From Latin purus, pure, and facio, to make — the root also of pure, purity, and purgatory (the last a corruption of the doctrine, not of the word).

Key Scripture

Acts 15:9 — "And put no difference between us and them, purifying their hearts by faith."

1 Peter 1:22 — "Seeing ye have purified your souls in obeying the truth through the Spirit unto unfeigned love of the brethren, see that ye love one another with a pure heart fervently:"

Titus 2:14 — "Who gave himself for us, that he might redeem us from all iniquity, and purify unto himself a peculiar people, zealous of good works."

1 John 3:3 — "And every man that hath this hope in him purifieth himself, even as he is pure."

Daniel 12:10 — "Many shall be purified, and made white, and tried; but the wicked shall do wickedly: and none of the wicked shall understand; but the wise shall understand."

Modern Corruption

Purgatory takes the word and moves the purifying beyond death into a place of satisfaction the believer must undergo himself, which denies that the blood of Christ purges the conscience once for all.

expand to see more

The Roman doctrine of purgatory holds that souls dying in grace but with temporal punishment still owing are purified by suffering before entering glory, and that the living may shorten that suffering by indulgences, masses, and almsgiving. The doctrine is built on 2 Maccabees, a book outside the Protestant canon, and on a reading of 1 Corinthians 3:15 that turns a statement about a builder’s work being burned into a statement about the builder being burned. Hebrews 9:14 says the blood of Christ shall purge your conscience from dead works, and Hebrews 10:14 that by one offering he hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified. If one offering perfected them for ever, there is no remainder for a furnace beyond death to consume, and the indulgence traffic that provoked Luther was the practical fruit of the error.

A second corruption is subtler and lives inside evangelical churches: the reduction of purity to sexual behaviour policed by pledges and rings, so that a young person is taught that purity is a status he keeps or forfeits by a single act. Acts 15:9 locates the purifying in the heart and assigns it to faith; 1 Peter 1:22 makes its object love of the brethren. Chastity is commanded and the dictionary does not soften it — but a purity culture that treats virginity as the thing purified has misplaced both the object and the agent, and it leaves the fallen with no gospel, since a status once forfeited cannot be restored by the scheme that defined it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek katharizo (G2511), to cleanse, to purify; hagnizo (G48), to purify ceremonially or morally; katharos (G2513), clean, pure; Hebrew taher (H2891), to be clean; barar (H1305), to purge, to make bright.

expand to see more

Greek katharizo (G2511) — to cleanse, to make clean; purifying their hearts by faith (Acts 15:9).

Greek hagnizo (G48) — to purify, akin to hagios, holy; used of the soul in 1 Peter 1:22 and of self-purifying hope in 1 John 3:3.

Greek katharos (G2513) — clean, unmixed; Blessed are the pure in heart (Matthew 5:8).

Hebrew taher (H2891) — to be clean, to purify; the Levitical word for the cleansed leper and the purged sanctuary.

Hebrew barar (H1305) — to purify, to make bright, to select; behind purified in Daniel 12:10.

Usage

"Purifying their hearts by faith (Acts 15:9) — the argument that ended the circumcision controversy."

"Purify unto himself a peculiar people (Titus 2:14) — the purchase and its purpose."

"Every man that hath this hope in him purifieth himself (1 John 3:3) — expectation of seeing Christ working backward into conduct."
